 Burleigh County ballot mistake did not affect results, election official says
 By 
 Michael Achterling 
 - 
 November 16, 2026 5:10 pm 
 Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County, speaks to the Burleigh County Canvassing Board while holding a stack of set-aside ballots on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
 A ballot mixup at Burleigh County polling location on Election Day would not have changed any election results, according to a county election official. 
 County canvassing boards met Monday to certify local election results ahead of North Dakota’s State Canvassing Board meeting Wednesday.  
 Dozens of voters in Burleigh County were given the wrong ballot by election judges at one Bismarck  polling location. 
 The ballots involved legislative candidates from District 7 on the northside of Bismarck. There were 134 District 7 voters who were given a ballot for District 8, which did not have any legislative candidates competing this year. 
 Election error caused some Bismarck voters to receive wrong ballot 
 Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, would go on to defeat her District 7 Democratic-NPL challenger Kevin Horneman 4,402 to 1,914. Republican House candidates Greg Vetter and Steve Sauter received 4,147 and 4,029, respectively, and defeated the Dem-NPL District 7 House candidates Tiffany Williams-Rice and Jason Thoms, who received 1,866 and 1,786 votes. 
 The margins of victory were large enough that the 134 votes would not have affected the outcomes.  
 “Essentially, the judges were giving out the wrong ballots,” said Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County.  
 The polling location had four different ballots that could have gone to voters depending on where they lived, he added. 
 “None of our other polling locations had this issue. It was an isolated situation,” Larson said. 
 Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County, speaks to the Burleigh County Canvassing Board on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor) 
 The mistake was discovered Election Day morning but voters were unable to change their ballots once they were inserted into the tabulation machines. 
 “Once a ballot is cast, there’s nothing you can do about it,” Larson said. He added the county plans to conduct more immersive training for election judges ahead of the 2028 election to ensure they are set up and prepared for the issue “not to happen again.” 
 He said the error at a single polling location does not reflect the accurate work of election workers across the county in the lead up to Election Day during the early voting period. 
 “At the Event Center, for 10 days during early voting and on Election Day, we have 33 different ballot styles there and this wasn’t an issue,” Larson said.
